title: Bhai Vir Singh
hookLine: a poet and novelist whose writing renewed Punjabi literature

cards: Some careful scholarship of the reform years came from people writing in English, for English readers. Bhai Vir Singh made a different bet.
He wrote in Punjabi, in Gurmukhi letters, for Punjabis: poems, novels, commentaries, tracts, a newspaper.
His work reads like a conviction that a people renews itself through its own language, and that Punjabi could carry beauty and faith as fully as English.

teach.h: BHAI: BROTHER, A TITLE OF RESPECT.
teach.b: First, the title. Bhai means brother. Sikhs give it to people respected for their learning and devotion, and it stuck to Vir Singh so firmly that it became part of his name.
Second, the range. He wrote short lyrics full of nature and longing for the Divine, and a long poem, Rana Surat Singh, about a widowed queen searching for peace.
He wrote novels set in the hard years of Sikh history, commentary on the Gurus' hymns, and worked on editions of older Sikh texts.
Some readers call him a father of modern Punjabi literature, though the title is a compliment, not a fact anyone can measure. Third, his tone.
In his short poems, the world is full of quiet signs: a flower on a mountainside, the sound of water, a bird. The feeling is longing, and then a glimpse of nearness.
It echoes the Gurus' own hymns, where Guru Nanak speaks of the creation as the place the Creator can be seen, dwelling in all of it. Fourth, why renewal. Reformers can argue and organize.

teach.h: SOMETHING TO LOVE, NOT ONLY ARGUE.
teach.b: But people also need something to love, words to read at night, a story that makes them proud.
Vir Singh gave the reform movement poems and novels, and gave Punjabi readers a reason to pick up their own language with joy.
He did it with the plainest tool there is: one more line, written in the language his readers dreamed in.

how: Bhai Vir Singh's poems and novels are read in Punjabi schools and Sikh homes, his commentaries are consulted by students of Gurbani, and his house in Amritsar is kept as a memorial.

practice: If you know a line of Punjabi poetry or Gurbani, say it once, quietly, and let it sit; if you don't, take a single word, Waheguru, and say it slowly, sound by sound, as if you'd never heard it before.
Then let it go silent, and just listen to the breath.
